Please read this carefully:

<document>
# A Cluster-Randomised Trial of a 30-Hour Week in Municipal Administration: Nine-Month Results

*Varden County Evaluation Unit, in collaboration with the Department of Labour Economics, Easterly University. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony and D. Rao. Registered protocol VC-2023-04.*

## Summary

We randomly assigned 24 administrative offices of a county government, employing 1,180 staff, to either reduce scheduled hours from 37.5 to 30 per week at full pay (12 offices) or continue on the standard schedule (12 offices) for nine months. Output was measured from administrative records, not from manager assessments, and actual hours from timesheets. The effect differed sharply by type of work. In case-processing offices, where work arrives as a backlog that can be cleared at any time, output per full-time employee changed by −2.1% (95% CI −6.8 to +2.6) relative to control and output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. In counter and contact-centre offices, where output depends on staff being present while the public is waiting, output per employee fell by 11.4% (95% CI −16.9 to −5.9), waiting times rose, and output per actual hour rose by a more modest 6.7%. Sick days fell by 29% across treated offices. An exploratory analysis suggests that a reduction in recurring meetings may account for part of the gain in case-processing offices.

## Motivation

Existing evidence on reduced working time comes mainly from voluntary pilots without comparison groups, in which output is often reported by the managers who sponsored the change. The county wished to know whether a reduced schedule could be extended to its own administrative staff without loss of service, and agreed to a randomised design with administrative output measures and a registered analysis plan.

## Design

**Units and randomisation.** The 24 offices were stratified into two strata by type of work before randomisation, and offices were randomised within strata:

- *Case-processing offices* (14 offices; 7 treated, 7 control): permits, licensing, benefits assessment and records. Work arrives as cases that join a queue and can be completed at any point within statutory deadlines.
- *Counter and contact-centre offices* (10 offices; 5 treated, 5 control): in-person service counters and telephone lines. Work arrives as members of the public who must be served while they wait.

Randomisation was at office level to avoid contamination between colleagues. Treated offices kept their public opening hours unchanged; staff rotas were rearranged so that each employee worked 30 scheduled hours.

**Outcomes.** The registered primary outcome is output per full-time-equivalent employee (FTE), measured as cases closed (case-processing) or contacts handled (counter and contact centre), from the county's case-management and telephony systems. Registered secondary outcomes are output per actual hour (from timesheets, which include any overtime claimed), quality (the share of decisions overturned on appeal; for contact centres, the repeat-contact rate within seven days), average waiting time, and sick days. Analysis is difference-in-differences against the six-month pre-period, with standard errors clustered by office.

**Exploratory measures.** At the request of office managers we also collected calendar data on recurring meetings in month six. This was not part of the registered plan.

## Results

### Hours

Scheduled hours fell by 20% in treated offices. Actual hours, from timesheets, fell by less: by 13% in case-processing offices (from 37.9 to 33.0 per week) and by 17% in counter offices (from 37.6 to 31.2), the difference reflecting overtime claimed to clear backlogs in case-processing. Control offices' actual hours were stable.

### Output and quality

**Table 1. Difference-in-differences estimates at nine months, treated relative to control**

| Outcome | Case-processing (7 v 7 offices) | Counter and contact centre (5 v 5 offices) |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −11.4% (−16.9 to −5.9) |
| Actual hours per FTE | −13% | −17% |
| Output per actual hour | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +6.7% (+0.4 to +13.3) |
| Appeal overturn rate / repeat contact rate | 3.1% v 3.0% | 11.8% v 10.9% |
| Average wait (minutes), treated offices, pre → month 9 | — | 4.2 → 6.9 |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% (both strata pooled) | |

In case-processing offices, output per employee was statistically indistinguishable from control, with a point estimate slightly below zero, and quality was unchanged. Because actual hours fell by 13%, output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. Measured against scheduled rather than actual hours, the gain would appear as 22%; we regard that figure as misleading, because staff did not in fact work only the scheduled hours.

In counter and contact-centre offices, the picture is different. With the same number of staff each working fewer hours, fewer staff were present at any given time during unchanged opening hours. Contacts handled per employee fell by 11.4% and the average wait rose from 4.2 to 6.9 minutes. Output per actual hour rose by 6.7%, but this did not offset the loss of hours, and the service the public received was worse. Abandoned calls rose from 6% to 10% of calls.

### Wellbeing

Sick days fell by 29% in treated offices relative to control. Resignations were lower in treated offices (annualised 3.9% against 7.4%), though with 12 offices per arm and few resignations the estimate is imprecise.

### Exploratory: meetings

Calendar data in month six showed that staff in treated case-processing offices spent 3.8 hours per week in recurring meetings against 7.1 hours in control case-processing offices, a difference of 3.3 hours. Offices that cut meetings most showed the largest gains in output per hour (correlation across the 7 treated offices, r = 0.71). Interviews suggested that the reduced schedule prompted managers to cancel standing meetings that had persisted by habit.

We emphasise that this analysis was not registered, that it rests on seven offices, and that a correlation across seven offices cannot establish a mechanism. We report it because, if confirmed, it would mean that a substantial part of the per-hour gain comes from removing low-value time rather than from rest alone, and that would matter for how the result is interpreted and for what other employers could expect. We have registered a confirmatory test for the 24-month follow-up.

## Discussion

Three conclusions follow from the registered analyses.

First, in work where output is not tied to presence, a 20% cut in scheduled hours produced a much smaller cut in actual hours and little or no measurable loss of output per employee. Output per hour rose by about an eighth.

Second, in work where output is tied to presence, the same change reduced output per employee by about a tenth and worsened service, even though each hour worked was somewhat more productive. Gains per hour do not by themselves imply that the hours reduction pays for itself. The question "does a shorter week raise productivity?" therefore has at least two answers depending on whether productivity is understood per hour or per employee, and these come apart most sharply in coverage-bound work.

Third, estimates computed against scheduled hours materially overstate the per-hour gain. In our data the overstatement is from 12.5% to 22% in case-processing offices.

These findings qualify claims, made on the basis of uncontrolled pilots, that reduced hours are sector-general. A sector may contain both kinds of work; what matters is whether output in a given role depends on hours of presence.

## Limitations

The trial is in one public employer, with 24 offices; confidence intervals are correspondingly wide, particularly in the counter stratum. Staff knew their assignment, and control staff knew that a trial was under way, which could have affected effort in either direction. Nine months may be too short to reveal whether gains persist after the novelty of the change wears off, or whether backlogs build up beyond the statutory deadlines. Public-sector case processing may differ from private-sector knowledge work in ways that affect the result. A 24-month follow-up is under way.

response:
I read the whole paper. This is a much stronger study than the previous pilot, and its headline conclusions are mostly well supported. Several things still need fixing, though: the paper reports no pooled primary estimate, the meeting analysis claims something its data can't show, the contact-centre numbers don't fully reconcile, and the inference with 10–14 clusters needs correcting.

## Arithmetic check

These all reproduce correctly:
- **Hours:** 33.0 / 37.9 is −12.9%, and 31.2 / 37.6 is −17.0%.
- **Output per actual hour:** case-processing gives 0.979 / 0.87 = +12.5%, and counter gives 0.886 / 0.83 = +6.7%.
- **Scheduled-hours comparison:** 0.979 / 0.8 = +22.4%.
- **Intervals:** the per-hour confidence intervals are roughly the output intervals divided by the hours ratio, so they're consistent.
- **Meetings:** 7.1 − 3.8 = 3.3 hours.

## What the paper does well

- It randomises within pre-specified strata and has a control group.
- Output comes from administrative records, and hours from timesheets.
- It registers its primary outcome and labels the exploratory analysis honestly.
- It reports the scheduled-hours estimate (+22%) and explains why it's misleading.
- The per-employee versus per-hour distinction is the right framing. It directly tests the "sector-general" claim that uncontrolled pilots make.

## Main issues

**1. The registered primary outcome is never reported for the whole sample.**
The protocol names a single primary outcome, output per FTE. The paper only reports it separately for each stratum. Stratifying the randomisation doesn't, by itself, pre-register a subgroup analysis.

The authors should:
- report the pooled estimate, which would be roughly −6% if weighted by office count;
- state whether the stratum-specific analysis appears in protocol VC-2023-04.

If it doesn't, the headline split is a post-hoc subgroup result, however plausible it is.

**2. The meeting correlation can't be calculated from the data described.**
Meeting data were collected only in month six. Without a pre-period measure, it's impossible to know which offices "cut meetings most." The r = 0.71 must actually relate the *level* of meetings at month six to the per-hour gain, and the authors should say so.

Similarly, the 3.3-hour gap is a cross-sectional comparison between treated and control offices, not a measured reduction. Randomisation makes it a reasonable proxy, but with only 7 offices per group, baseline imbalance is possible.

There is also a point that supports the authors' hypothesis. If the two groups had similar meeting time at baseline, then:
- non-meeting hours fell from about 30.8 to 29.2 per week, around −5%;
- output fell only 2.1%;
- so output per non-meeting hour rose about 3%.

Under that assumption, removing meetings could account for most of the 12.5% gain, not just "part" of it. That is worth saying, with the assumption stated, and it strengthens the case for the registered confirmatory test.

**3. The contact-centre numbers don't add up.**
Calls handled can only fall because of abandonment if public demand stayed the same. Abandonment rose from 6% to 10%, so the share of calls answered fell from 94% to 90%, a drop of about 4%. That doesn't explain an 11.4% fall in contacts handled.

Something else is happening, and the paper doesn't say what. Possibilities include:
- fewer people coming to the counters;
- people giving up before joining the queue;
- people being redirected to other channels;
- a mix of outputs from counters and phones that the paper doesn't separate.

Demand, meaning arrivals and calls offered, should be reported alongside contacts handled.

**4. In queue-based work, "output per hour" partly measures how busy staff are.**
In contact centres, output depends on how many people arrive. With fewer staff on duty, each hour is busier and waits get longer. The 6.7% per-hour "gain" may largely be reduced idle time rather than improved efficiency. The Discussion's statement that "each hour worked was somewhat more productive" should acknowledge this.

A similar concern applies to case-processing. Staff may close easier cases first, or the backlog may grow while the number of closures holds steady. The authors should report:
- backlog size;
- case age;
- the share of cases closed within statutory deadlines.

The Limitations section mentions this risk, but the data to check it should already exist in the case-management system.

**5. The statistical intervals are probably too narrow.**
Standard errors clustered by office are unreliable with very few clusters. Here there are 14 offices in one stratum and 10 in the other (5 per arm), and conventional cluster-robust standard errors understate uncertainty badly at those numbers. The authors should use one of:
- the wild cluster bootstrap;
- randomisation inference, which fits a randomised design naturally;
- small-sample corrections, such as CR2 with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom.

With 5 offices per arm, the contact-centre interval of −16.9% to −5.9% in particular may widen considerably.

**6. Several registered secondary outcomes aren't analysed as registered.**
The protocol says difference-in-differences, but:
- **Waiting time** is shown only as treated offices before and after (4.2 → 6.9 minutes), with no control comparison.
- **Abandoned calls** (6% → 10%) aren't a registered outcome and are given only in the text, with no control comparison.
- **Quality** is shown as "3.1% v 3.0%" and "11.8% v 10.9%" with no estimate of the difference, no interval, and no indication of which figure belongs to the treated group. The contact-centre repeat-contact gap of 0.9 points isn't mentioned in the text, even though it would add to the worse-service finding.
- **Sick days and resignations** have no intervals, and sick days are only reported pooled across both strata.

**7. Timesheets capture claimed hours, not hours actually worked.**
Unpaid extra work (finishing tasks at home, working through breaks) wouldn't show up. If it happened, the per-hour gains are overstated, which is the same problem the paper rightly criticises in scheduled-hours estimates.

Claimed overtime is also paid on top of unchanged salaries, so the trial has a cost the paper never reports. The county's actual question was whether the change can be made "without loss of service." Answering it needs:
- cost per case and cost per contact;
- the extra staff that would be needed to restore counter coverage.

## Smaller points

- **"Statistically indistinguishable" is not "no loss."** In case-processing, the interval for output per employee runs from −6.8% to +2.6%. It can't rule out a loss of nearly 7%. The phrase "little or no measurable loss" should report the smallest effect the trial could detect, or be softened.
- **How the 30 hours were scheduled isn't stated.** If staff worked four days instead of five, part of the 29% fall in sick days is mechanical, since there are fewer working days on which to be off sick.
- **Contamination between offices isn't ruled out.** The paper should say whether offices share a county-wide case queue or phone system. If they do, work could have shifted from treated to control offices.
- **Behaviour in control offices could have changed.** Control staff knew about the trial and might have worked harder to compete, or less hard out of resentment. The authors could check whether control offices' output and hours changed compared with the period before the trial.
- **Staff numbers by stratum** (of the 1,180 total) should be reported.
- **One sentence is unclear.** "The overstatement is from 12.5% to 22%" would be clearer as: "the scheduled-hours estimate (22%) is nearly double the actual-hours estimate (12.5%)."

## Bottom line

The core findings are credible and important:
- Cutting hours costs little output per employee in work cleared from a backlog.
- It worsens service in work that depends on staff being present, unless more staff are added.
- Measuring against scheduled hours roughly doubles the apparent per-hour gain.

The fixes the paper needs are to report the pooled primary estimate, correct the inference for the small number of offices, and reconcile the contact-centre figures. It should also describe the meeting analysis accurately, and add backlog and cost data so the county can answer its own question.

I can draft referee comments or write the small-cluster reanalysis plan if useful.
